title: If and then
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: ONE ENDING COVERS if AND whenever. -(eu)myeon is the whole conditional: Sigan-i isseumyeon gachi gayo is both 'if you have time' and 'whenever you have time', and only what is around it decides which. M3's hoksi may stand in front to mark the doubtful reading, and in speech it is optional.

THE ENDING PICKS ITS SHAPE FROM THE STEM, NOT FROM THE MEANING. A stem ending in a vowel takes -myeon: gamyeon, omyeon, hamyeon, apeumyeon. A stem ending in a consonant takes -eumyeon: isseumyeon, eopseumyeon, joeumyeon. It is welded on with no hyphen, because in this course a hyphen means a particle and nothing else.

THE CONDITION COMES FIRST, ALWAYS. English is free to trail it — 'take some medicine if your head hurts' — and Korean is not. The -(eu)myeon clause opens the sentence and the main clause finishes it. There is no shape in which the two are reversed.

PROHIBITION IS THE CONDITIONAL PLUS L2-M8's an dwaeyo. Neutge gamyeon an dwaeyo is literally 'if you go late, it does not become'. The negation belongs to dwaeyo and never to the condition: an gamyeon dwaeyo would say the opposite — that not going is fine.

THE WISH IS THE CONDITIONAL PLUS joayo. Nalssi-ga joeumyeon joayo is 'if the weather is good, it is good', and that is how Korean hopes for something. There is no verb for hoping anywhere in it, which is why an English speaker never guesses this shape.

ADVICE IS ASSEMBLED FROM WHAT THE COURSE ALREADY OWNS. -neun ge eottaeyo? is M2's modifier, the noun-maker ge and L2-M6's eottaeyo; direct advice is L2-M1's -(eu)seyo; obligation is L2-M8's -eoya dwaeyo. This module reaches back three times and forward none, and the -(eu)seyo lines chip formal while everything else stays neutral.

WHAT THIS MODULE DOES NOT OPEN. The past counterfactual — if I had gone, I would have seen it — is L4-M3's. -(eu)myeonseo, meaning while, is L4-M6's. Conjecture with -gess- is L3-M6's. And 'let us' is -(eu)psida, which belongs to the -mnida speech level and travels with it to L4-M7: a suggestion here is L2-M6's -(eu)llae-yo or the advice frame, never that.

sentences.cue: If you have time, let's go together.

words.cue: if there is · whenever there is
words.note: L1-M3's isseoyo with -(eu)myeon. The stem iss- ends in a consonant, so the ending brings its eu along: isseumyeon, never issmyeon.

sentences.trap: ONE ENDING, TWO ENGLISH WORDS. This sentence is 'if you have time' and 'whenever you have time' at once. Korean has nothing to choose between, so a learner looking for the difference is looking for something that is not there.
sentences.sound: SI-ga-ni I-sseu-myeon GA-chi GA-yo. isseumyeon is said i-sseu-myeon, and gachi is said ga-chi.

variations.cue: If you have time, let's eat together.
variations.changed: L1-M3's meogeoyo as the main clause

variations.cue: If by any chance you have time, give me a call.
variations.changed: M3's hoksi in front, which marks the doubtful reading

mistake.why: There is no separate word for 'if'. The ending is welded onto the stem: Sigan-i isseumyeon gachi gayo.

sentences.usage: Inviting somebody without putting them on the spot.
sentences.mnemonic: if and whenever are one ending.

sentences.cue: Whenever it rains, I rest at home.

words.cue: if it comes · whenever it comes
words.note: M3's bi-ga wayo built on the stem o-, which ends in a vowel, so the ending is the plain -myeon: omyeon.

sentences.trap: THIS IS THE SAME ENDING AS S01, READ THE OTHER WAY. Nothing in the Korean marks a habit rather than a one-off; the main clause is a habit, so the condition is read as 'whenever'. Put hoksi in front and the same words become 'if'.

variations.cue: Whenever it rains, I take a taxi.
variations.changed: a different habit in the main clause

variations.cue: Whenever it rains, I stay at home.
variations.changed: L1-M3's isseoyo, with L1-M7's -e for being somewhere

mistake.why: Rain arriving in the account is news, so it takes -ga: Bi-ga omyeon jip-eseo swieoyo. With -neun it would be the topic of the whole sentence, which M1's law does not allow here.

sentences.usage: Describing what you usually do in bad weather.
sentences.mnemonic: Same ending, the context reads it.

sentences.cue: You mustn't be late for the meeting.

words.note: L1-M4's gayo with -myeon. The stem ga- ends in a vowel, so no eu is added — the same reason omyeon and hamyeon look the way they do.

sentences.trap: KOREAN FORBIDS BY SAYING IT DOES NOT BECOME. There is no word for 'must not' here at all: the prohibition is this module's condition plus L2-M8's an dwaeyo, assembled out of two things you already have.
sentences.sound: HOE-ui-e NEUT-ge GA-myeon an DWAE-yo. neutge is said neut-kke.

variations.cue: You mustn't be late for school.
variations.changed: school rather than the meeting

variations.cue: You mustn't go late.
variations.changed: no place named at all — the bare prohibition

mistake.why: The negation belongs to dwaeyo, not to the condition. As written this says the opposite — that not going late is fine. Hoeui-e neutge gamyeon an dwaeyo.

sentences.usage: Telling a colleague what the rule is.

sentences.cue: You mustn't make phone calls at school.

words.note: L1-M4's haeyo with -myeon, on the stem ha-. Every -hada verb builds its condition this way, so gongbuhamyeon and jeonhwahamyeon come free with it.

sentences.trap: THE eu IS NOT A CHOICE. A stem ending in a vowel takes -myeon and a stem ending in a consonant takes -eumyeon. haeumyeon is not a milder or more careful version of hamyeon; it is not a shape the language has.

variations.cue: You mustn't make phone calls here.
variations.changed: L2-M1's yeogi-eseo, so the rule is about this room

variations.cue: It's fine if you do it at home.
variations.changed: dwaeyo without the an — permission instead of prohibition

mistake.why: The stem ha- ends in a vowel, so it takes the plain -myeon: Hakgyo-eseo jeonhwa-reul hamyeon an dwaeyo.

sentences.usage: Saying what is not allowed somewhere.

sentences.cue: How about going to the hospital?

words.note: L1-M4's gayo wearing M2's present modifier -neun. Nothing new is opened here; the modifier is doing exactly what ilhaneun and haneun already did.

words.cue: the thing of — turns a clause into a noun
words.note: It follows a modifier and makes the whole clause into a thing, which eottaeyo can then ask about. A finished -yo verb can never stand in front of it.

sentences.trap: ADVICE IN KOREAN ASKS ABOUT A THING. English asks about an action — 'how about going' — and Korean builds the going into a noun with ge first, then asks how that thing is. The modifier ending is what makes the noun possible.

variations.cue: How about going to the hospital tomorrow?
variations.changed: a day added in front of the clause

variations.cue: Going to the hospital is the good option.
variations.changed: joayo instead of the question — advice stated rather than offered

mistake.why: ge follows the MODIFIER, exactly as M3's geot gatayo does: Byeongwon-e ganeun ge eottaeyo?

sentences.usage: Suggesting something to a friend who is unwell.

sentences.cue: If your head hurts, take some medicine.

words.note: L2-M8's apayo with -myeon. The stem is apeu-, which ends in a vowel, so the eu here is the stem's own and not the ending's.

sentences.trap: THE CONDITION CANNOT TRAIL. English says 'take some medicine if your head hurts' just as happily as the other order; Korean has only the one order, with the condition opening the sentence.
sentences.sound: MEO-ri-ga A-peu-myeon YA-geul DEU-se-yo. yak-eul is said ya-geul.

variations.cue: If your stomach hurts, go to the hospital.
variations.changed: L2-M5's bae, and L2-M4's gaseyo as the advice

variations.cue: If your head hurts, rest at home.
variations.changed: a plain -yo main clause instead of the honorific one

mistake.why: The condition opens the sentence: Meori-ga apeumyeon yak-eul deuseyo. Korean never trails it after the main clause.

sentences.usage: Advising somebody older or senior who is unwell.

sentences.cue: If there's no time, we have to go now.

words.note: L1-M3's eopseoyo with -(eu)myeon. The stem eops- ends in a consonant, so it takes the eu shape, exactly as isseumyeon does.

sentences.trap: THE OBLIGATION IS NOT NEW. gaya dwaeyo is L2-M8's, unchanged and unhyphenated; all this module adds is a condition in front of it. Korean did not grow a second way to say 'have to' for conditional sentences.
sentences.sound: SI-ga-ni EOP-seu-myeon JI-geum GA-ya DWAE-yo. eopseumyeon is said eop-sseu-myeon.

variations.cue: If there's no time, take a taxi.
variations.changed: advice instead of obligation

variations.cue: If there's time, rest at home.
variations.changed: the positive condition, on the same noun

mistake.why: The -eoya is not optional: Sigan-i eopseumyeon jigeum gaya dwaeyo.

sentences.usage: Deciding out loud when the clock has run down.

sentences.cue: You don't have time? Then take a taxi.

words.note: The same stem as M3's geureoke, wearing this module's -myeon: literally 'if that is so'. It is the one place the conditional stands alone as a whole word.

sentences.trap: KOREAN'S 'THEN' IS A CONDITIONAL. geureomyeon is not a sequencing word like L2-M10's geu daeum-e — it takes what the other person just said and makes it the condition of what you are about to say.

variations.cue: You have time? Then let's go together.
variations.changed: the opposite answer, and an invitation after it

variations.cue: Then shall we go tomorrow?
variations.changed: L2-M6's -(eu)llae-yo, which is this course's way of suggesting

mistake.why: geureoke is 'that way' and says how something is done. 'Then' is the conditional: Geureomyeon taeksi-reul taseyo.

sentences.usage: Reacting to what somebody has just told you.

sentences.cue: I really hope the weather is good tomorrow.

words.note: The weather. It is what M3's bi arrives in, and it takes -ga here because it is the subject of the condition rather than the topic of the sentence.
L1-M9's joayo with -(eu)myeon. The stem joh- ends in a consonant, so the eu shape is used and the h is not heard: jo-eu-myeon.

sentences.trap: KOREAN HOPES BY SAYING 'IF X, GOOD'. There is no verb for hoping in this sentence. English needs one and puts it first; Korean builds the wish out of the condition it already has, with joayo closing it.

variations.cue: I hope it doesn't rain.
variations.changed: L1-M3's short an inside the condition

variations.cue: If the weather is good tomorrow, let's go together.
variations.changed: an ordinary condition instead of the wish

mistake.why: The wish is built on the CONDITIONAL: Naeil nalssi-ga joeumyeon jeongmal joayo. A finished verb cannot stand in the condition slot.

sentences.usage: Saying what you are hoping for, without asking for it.
sentences.mnemonic: If it is good, it is good.

sentences.display: Maeil undonghaneun ge eottaeyo? Geureomyeon jeongmal joayo.
sentences.script: 매일 운동하는 게 어때요? 그러면 정말 좋아요.
sentences.cue: How about exercising every day? Then it's really good.
sentences.literal: every-day exercising thing how-is? if-that-is-so really is-good

words.note: M1's undonghaeyo wearing M2's present modifier. Every -hada verb builds it the same way, which is why ge can be hung on any of them.

sentences.trap: 'LET'S' IS NOT AVAILABLE HERE. The ending an English speaker reaches for is -(eu)psida, and it belongs to the formal speech level this course does not speak. Korean offers the idea as a question instead, and that is what -neun ge eottaeyo? is for.
sentences.sound: MAE-il un-dong-HA-neun ge eo-TTAE-yo? geu-REO-myeon JEONG-mal JO-a-yo.

variations.cue: How about exercising every day?
variations.changed: the advice on its own, with nothing after it

variations.cue: Exercising often is the good option.
variations.changed: M1's jaju, and the advice stated rather than offered

mistake.why: -(eu)psida belongs to the formal speech level, which this course does not teach. The suggestion is Maeil undonghaneun ge eottaeyo?

sentences.usage: Offering somebody a change of habit without pushing it.

comprehensionPool.cue: If you have time, let's go together.
Whenever it rains, I rest at home.
You mustn't be late for the meeting.
You mustn't make phone calls at school.
How about going to the hospital?
If your head hurts, take some medicine.
If there's no time, we have to go now.
You don't have time? Then take a taxi.
I really hope the weather is good tomorrow.
If your stomach hurts, go to the hospital.
